Deaths entered the count as allegations, from a national register at St George's, University of London, that receives information on drug-related deaths from coroners and, in Scotland, procurators fiscal (the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths), from internet searches of toxicology, newspaper and media websites, and from a toxicology group; media reports filled gaps where coroners' files could not be seen. The register admits a death if a drug was directly implicated, the person had a history of drug dependence or misuse, or a controlled drug was found after death, so a death could enter because mephedrone was present (Schifano et al., 2012). A 'confirmed' death meant that mephedrone was identified, not that it caused the death, as the authors state; one of the 62, who died in hospital three weeks after taking it, had none found after death. Other substances were found in 54 of the 62, most often alcohol (26), other stimulants (22) and sleeping or calming medicines (22); by the authors' grouping, 26 deaths were drug poisonings with mephedrone alone or with other substances, 18 were self-inflicted (11 by hanging), 6 followed risky behaviour such as trying to swim a river, driving or a stabbing, 5 followed collapse at a party, 5 occurred in hospital days or weeks later and 2 followed risky sexual activity; the coroners' or procurators fiscal's verdicts were accident or misadventure in 35, suicide in 11, open in 8, 'abuse of drugs' in 5 and homicide, natural causes and a narrative verdict in 1 each (Schifano et al., 2012). set.statement: By 31 October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK, Channel Islands and Isle of Man had been alleged to be associated with mephedrone. Tests after death found no mephedrone in 25 (19.5%, editors’ calculation), and 13 results were pending. The Results describe 90 as positive, 69 with concluded inquests, and 62 with forms received and analysed (Schifano et al., 2012). This flow has an exception: Table 2 says one of the 62 died in hospital three weeks after taking mephedrone and had none found after death. The paper mentions ante-mortem findings collectively but does not give this person’s individual confirmation evidence. A negative test after death does not establish no earlier exposure. The cases came from the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths, internet searches of toxicology and news sites, and a toxicology group. Coroners and Scottish procurators fiscal supplied records; media reports sometimes filled gaps. The register admits deaths with a directly implicated psychoactive substance, a history of dependence or misuse, or a controlled drug present after death. Presence of mephedrone itself could meet the last criterion only after its classification, which the paper dates to spring 2010; the entry criterion for each death is not stated (editors’ reading; Schifano et al., 2012). Mephedrone was the only substance identified in 8 of 62. The remaining 54 (62−8, editors’ calculation) were outside that only-substance group; this subtraction does not establish an individual co-detection result for the post-mortem-negative exception. Alcohol 26, other stimulants 22 and hypnotics or sedatives 22 were the most common other categories. Categories overlap and do not identify which substance caused a death. Mephedrone was formally named in the recorded cause in 36, on its own in 18. Who made those causal decisions and what evidence or rules they used are unstated (Schifano et al., 2012). The authors separately grouped 26 deaths as acute drug toxicity, 18 as self-inflicted harm, 6 as risky behaviour, 5 as collapse at a party, 5 as delayed hospital deaths and 2 as risky sexual activity. Those circumstance groups differ from the legal verdicts: 35 accident or misadventure, 11 suicide, 8 open, 5 drug misuse, and 1 each homicide, natural causes and narrative. The paper does not reconcile 18 self-inflicted deaths with 11 suicide verdicts; neither classification establishes that mephedrone caused self-harm (Schifano et al., 2012). The authors explicitly distinguish detection from causation and caution that failure to detect mephedrone may reflect test limitations. They regard the count as a minimum because some positive cases awaited inquest, geographical reporting was incomplete and tests varied. About 95% of coroners’ areas in England and Wales reported regularly; this is not 95% completeness of deaths across the UK. Untested or unalleged deaths could also be missed (editors’ inference, not a measured source finding). The Discussion names blood for the quantified levels, but blood type, sampling site and time, laboratory methods and panels are not described. With no count of use, this series supplies no death rate. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
set.plain: How many deaths linked to mephedrone were confirmed? By October 2011, 128 deaths had been alleged in the UK and nearby islands. One person died weeks later in hospital and had none found after death; the paper does not explain their individual earlier test evidence. expect.statement: Deaths recorded as heroin 'overdoses' often involve other drugs, delays and other mechanisms, so the label does not show that heroin alone caused the death, but which substance or mechanism was decisive in a given death cannot be read from the toxicology. In a 1996 narrative review of medical examiners' and coroners' series and official statistics, mostly from 1967 to 1996 in the USA, Australia and Europe, chosen by the authors without a stated search and leaning on their own New South Wales series of 152 heroin-related deaths in 1992, morphine (the substance heroin becomes in the body) was the only drug detected at autopsy in 23% to 48% of deaths attributed to heroin overdose across six studies; alcohol was detected in 29% to 75% across 13 studies, with mean blood alcohol of 0.09 to 0.16 g/100 mL where reported, and benzodiazepines in 12% to 55% across four; which drugs each laboratory looked for, and how each source defined a heroin death, is not given (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand). Blood morphine was lower in deaths with alcohol in the five studies that compared them, with weak correlations where reported (r = −0.14 in 505 deaths; r = −0.28 in the authors' series); a third of the authors' series had morphine below the laboratories' toxic level for people without opioid tolerance (0.16 mg/L); and a 1977 Michigan series found 74% with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes (Darke & Zador, 1996). Many deaths were not instant: 14% of the authors' series were classed as instant and 22% took more than 3 hours, other series found intervals of more than 2 or 3 hours in 44% and 52%, and other people were present at more than half of the deaths in four studies (58% to 79% where a figure was given; Darke & Zador, 1996). The reviewers write that 'overdose' 'may correctly apply to only a minority of heroin-related deaths' and propose 'multiple drug toxicity' for many of them; but finding other drugs does not show that they caused the death, the comparison with survivors rests on three studies cited without figures, tolerance was measured in no study, and low morphine can also reflect a death hours after the last injection, when morphine had already fallen, or change after death (Darke & Zador, 1996). In England and Wales in 2000, of 1,037 accidental drug-related deaths that coroners reported to a national register (the National Programme of Substance Abuse Deaths; reporting voluntary, coverage not stated), the register's researchers classed 802 (77%) as direct overdoses and 235 (23%) as other mechanisms: choking on stomach contents and other acute events (74), drug toxicity on top of a medical condition (112), injuries (31) and infections (18). Heroin or morphine was named as implicated in 424 of the direct overdoses and found after death in 488, and was implicated in 42 of the 74 acute events, 33 of the 72 deaths with a drug-related medical condition and 11 of the 18 infections; alcohol was found after death in 316 (39.4%) of the direct overdoses; methadone was implicated in 13% of direct overdoses but was the only drug implicated in 4%. These figures are the researchers' reading of coroners' returns that recorded only drugs found, not a check of official statistics, which were not compared (Webb et al., 2003). In the other direction, heroin can be missed: 6-MAM, the marker that shows heroin rather than another source of morphine, fell in femoral blood after death in bodies sampled more than once (Borra et al., 2026), and a review table reports, second-hand, that testing the fluid around the brain and spinal cord for 6-MAM detected 46% more heroin-related deaths than testing blood (Leikin & Watson, 2003). The evidence is old (before fentanyl), largely second-hand, and from series chosen by the authors or from a register. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

set.statement: Other drugs are often detected in deaths labelled heroin overdose, but detection does not establish which substances caused a death. A 1996 narrative review, with no stated search or appraisal, selected medical-examiner and coroner series and statistics from the USA, Australia and Europe, mostly published 1967–1996, leaning on the authors’ 152 deaths in New South Wales in 1992. It relays morphine as the only drug detected in 23%–48% across six series and alcohol in 29%–75% across 13, with mean blood alcohol 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL where reported. Diazepam alone was detected in 12% in one study; three others reported benzodiazepines in 22%, 27% and 55%. These are second-hand findings with unknown laboratory panels and varying death definitions, not shares proved to have been caused by heroin alone or by combinations (Darke & Zador, 1996). Five cited studies reported lower blood morphine when alcohol was detected. Correlations were weak where given: −0.14 in 505 alcohol-positive deaths and −0.28 in the authors’ series. A third of their series was below the laboratories’ 0.16 mg/L toxic level for people without opioid tolerance. A Michigan series published in 1977 reported 74% with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died from other causes; the review does not establish its case-collection dates. It cites three survivor comparisons without numerical results and says better living-versus-fatal comparisons would add substantially to knowledge (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand). In the authors’ series 14% were classed as instant deaths and 22% took more than 3 hours; other series reported 44% beyond 2 hours and 52% beyond 3 hours. Other people were present in more than half of deaths in four studies (58%–79% where specified). The reviewers infer that combined drug toxicity explains many deaths. The editors’ limitation is that presence alone does not establish causal shares, tolerance was not measured, and delayed death is another possible explanation for low morphine. Darke and Zador do not discuss post-mortem redistribution; that separate limitation comes from toxicology literature, not their conclusions. The post-mortem result alone cannot decide the cause (Darke & Zador, 1996; Borra et al., 2026). In England and Wales in 2000, researchers reclassified1,037 accidental drug-related deaths voluntarily reported by coroners to a register of unstated completeness. They assigned 802 (77%) to direct overdose and 235 (23%) to other categories: 74 acute physical events, 112 toxicity with a medical condition, 31 traumatic accidents and 18 acute infections. Direct overdose was the default when no evidence suggested otherwise. Thus 77% is an upper bound for that default category and 23% a lower bound for alternatives under this record-based scheme—not a validated misclassification rate or a comparison with official statistics (editors’ reading; Webb et al., 2003). Heroin/morphine was recorded as implicated in 424 of 802 direct overdoses and detected in 488; it was implicated in 42 of 74 acute physical events, 33 of 72 deaths with a drug-related medical condition, and 11 of 18 infections. Alcohol was detected in 316 of 802 direct overdoses (39.4%), but the register recorded it only alongside other drugs. Methadone was implicated in 13% of direct overdoses, as the sole implicated drug in 4%; sole implication does not mean no other drug was detected. Negative findings were not recorded, leaving absence versus lack of testing uncertain (Webb et al., 2003). Heroin exposure can also be missed. A review reports falling femoral-blood 6-MAM, a heroin marker, between post-mortem samples in one primary study. It also relays both higher and lower post-mortem opioid concentrations compared with samples from life, with additional timing, specimen and morphine-transformation limits (Borra et al., 2026). Another review’s table says cerebrospinal-fluid 6-MAM detected 46% more heroin-related cases than blood, but supplies no case counts or unique per-value primary citation; this is a second-hand testing comparison, not 46% more proven heroin-caused deaths (Leikin & Watson, 2003). The main death-series figures are historical and cannot describe current drug mixtures or yield a rate per use. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: Are deaths labelled heroin overdose always caused by heroin alone? Other drugs were often found in the older studies, but that does not show which caused a death. expect.statement: No blood level of MDMA can be named as fatal from these studies: levels in deaths put down to MDMA were higher on average but overlapped widely with levels in people who died of other causes with MDMA in their blood, and in one early series people died with lower levels than a person who had only mild symptoms. In 77 deaths with MDMA or a related drug found at full autopsy in Sheffield, England, in 1992 to 2008 (one department's files; causes given by certifiers the paper does not name, on criteria it does not state), 17 deaths were put down principally to MDMA, 30 to several drugs together and 28 to injuries; femoral-blood MDMA ranged from 0.478 to 53.9 mg/L (median 3.49) in the 13 MDMA deaths with a blood value, from 0.04 to 41.5 mg/L (median 0.76) in 22 deaths from several drugs, and from 0.035 to 4.81 mg/L (median 0.483) in 24 deaths from injuries such as homicide, vehicle collisions, falls and drowning; the median was about 7 times higher in deaths put down to MDMA, but at least 7 of those 13 values lay within the range of the injury deaths (editors' calculations from the printed medians and ranges; Milroy, 2011). The author concludes that there is no specific toxic or fatal MDMA level and that a level cannot give the cause of death without the history and the other autopsy findings; he treats the injury deaths as a stand-in for levels after ordinary use, 'likely to equate with those of normal recreational use', which was not measured, and notes that deaths from drinking too much water can show low levels because the blood is diluted; whoever gave the causes probably knew the levels, which would exaggerate the difference between the groups rather than the overlap (Milroy, 2011). One death in that series in which samples were taken two days after death, as cited from another study, had heart blood about four times its femoral blood (Milroy, 2011, second-hand). In 7 deaths of people aged 16 to 21 reported to the London poisons information service in 1990 and 1991, after taking, by report, 1 to 5 tablets of unknown content, or an unstated number, at clubs, parties or a concert, with body temperatures of 40 to 43°C, plasma MDMA was 0.11 to 1.26 mg/L in the 5 with a measured value, while one person with 7.72 mg/L had only mild symptoms; when the samples were taken is not stated (Henry et al., 1992). In Finland, MDMA was found in femoral blood in 57 medico-legal autopsies of all causes in 2000 to 2010 (median 0.30 mg/L, 97.5th percentile 4.0 mg/L), and forensic pathologists certified none of them as MDMA poisoning (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). A narrative review records published 'lethal' MDMA ranges of 40 to 8,500 µg/L (0.04 to 8.5 mg/L), second-hand (Ferner, 2008), and MDMA is among the drugs found higher in femoral blood after death than in samples taken in life (Borra et al., 2026, relayed without sizes; see the answer on whether levels change after death). None of these studies measured MDMA in living people after ordinary use. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

set.statement: These studies do not establish a blood-MDMA cutoff that separates death caused by MDMA from other deaths or survival. They show overlap, while differing in population, specimen and sampling time. A Sheffield department reviewed 77 autopsies with MDMA or related compounds detected in 1992–2008. Of the full series, 17 deaths were attributed principally to MDMA, 30 to several drugs and 28 to trauma, with 2 other deaths. The blood-value subsets were 13, 22 and 24 respectively. Femoral-blood MDMA ranged 0.478–53.9 mg/L (median 3.49), 0.04–41.5 (median 0.76) and 0.035–4.81 (median 0.483). The toxicity median was about 7.2 times the trauma median; at least 7 of 13 toxicity values fall within the trauma range (editors’ calculations from the order statistics and ranges, not individual data; Milroy, 2011). The author concludes that concentration needs the history and full autopsy findings. He treats trauma deaths as a proxy for ordinary-use levels, but no living ordinary-use group was measured and MDMA could have contributed to a collision, fall or drowning. Certifiers, attribution rules and their knowledge of concentrations are not reported. If high levels influenced classification, the observed separation could partly reflect that decision; this is the editors’ possible-bias explanation, not Milroy’s documented method. He also notes possible low levels after water intoxication through dilution (Milroy, 2011). A striking specimen comparison cited by Milroy belongs to Elliott’s separate study of deaths after hospital admission, not the Sheffield 77. In one case sampled 2 days after death, heart blood 28.39 mg/L was about 3.9–4.6 times the two femoral values 6.19 and 7.25; an earlier serum value 4.33 had been taken a day before death. These are second-hand values from different sites, times and matrices, not an isolated measure of redistribution (Milroy, 2011, reporting Elliott). Henry et al. reported 7 deaths aged 16–21 among London poisons-service enquiries in 1990–1991. Recorded temperatures were 40–43°C; plasma MDMA was 0.11–1.26 mg/L in 5 quantified fatal cases, with sampling times unstated. The paper also gives 8 survivor values: 5 after severe complications (including a child’s accidental exposure) and 3 after road accidents. Together they ranged 0.05–0.97 mg/L and overlapped the fatal range; all 5 severe-case values lay inside it (editors’ comparison of Tables I–III). These are selected hospital plasma measurements, not post-mortem femoral blood or healthy ordinary use. The separate 7.72 mg/L case has only a short description of hangover, tachycardia and hypertension, with sampling time and detailed follow-up unstated; it cannot define a tolerated range (Henry et al., 1992). A previously checked Finnish source extraction records 57 medico-legal autopsies of all causes with MDMA in femoral blood in 2000–2010, median 0.30 mg/L and 97.5th percentile 4.0; its table prints 0% fatal poisoning with MDMA as the main finding (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014; primary full text unavailable in this continuation). That category excludes other possible contributions. With 57 cases, one would round to 2%, so ordinary whole-percent rounding is consistent with none in that specific category (editors’ arithmetic), not proof of no MDMA contribution. A narrative review relays one published lethal-MDMA range of 40–8,500 µg/L, equivalent to 0.04–8.5 mg/L (Ferner, 2008, second-hand). Borra et al. report higher femoral MDMA after death than earlier plasma or serum, without effect sizes; elimination before death, incomplete absorption or distribution, possible later administration, hospital selection and specimen differences prevent attributing each difference solely to redistribution (2026). None of these findings supplies a validated ordinary-use comparison or fatal cutoff. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

expect.statement: 'Excited delirium' is a contested label rather than a recognized diagnosis, and evidence is insufficient to say whether the state it describes kills without restraint, or how far deaths given the label were caused by restraint, by drugs such as cocaine, or by both. It is not in the international classification of diseases (ICD) or the psychiatric manual (DSM), has no validated diagnostic criteria and no autopsy or laboratory finding specific to it, and is applied as a diagnosis of exclusion, mainly in medico-legal reports of deaths of agitated people during or after police restraint or in custody (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026; Strömmer et al., 2020). In the published case literature the label was used mostly by forensic pathologists, and also by emergency physicians and others, and a 2012 defining review and a 2009 emergency physicians' white paper gave fatality figures for it (under 10% and 8.3%) that the authors of the pooled analysis below trace to a study without any death figures (Strömmer et al., 2020). The authors of both reviews read here reject the term: one team proposes 'agitated delirium' with a note of the presence and degree of restraint, and recording the manner of death of restrained people as homicide or undetermined rather than natural or accident (Strömmer et al., 2020); the other uses 'acute behavioral disturbance' and reports critics' view that the label deflects attention from restraint and is applied with racial bias (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026). In a pooled analysis of 168 published cases (English-language case reports and series to April 2020), 92 of 120 cases labelled 'excited delirium' had died, against 12 of 48 labelled 'agitated delirium'; some force, from manual restraint and handcuffs to electrical weapons or sedation, was recorded in 94 of the 104 deaths, only 3 of the 168 cases had no force recorded (2 of them died), and cocaine was noted in 55 of the 104 deaths and 19 of the 64 survivors, as the case reports described it rather than as toxicology results (Strömmer et al., 2020). Its authors read this as no evidence that excited delirium kills without restraint; but their own introduction notes that forensic reports describe deaths and use 'excited delirium' while clinical reports describe survivors, so the label, death and the recording of restraint travel together by type of source, which the analysis did not take into account, and the authors later corrected one table (Strömmer et al., 2020, and the first reader's appraisal). A 2026 systematic review of deaths in custody (searches for 2010 to 2025) describes restraint deaths mostly in young or middle-aged men, often with obesity and stimulant intoxication, names cocaine, methamphetamine and phencyclidine as 'frequently identified in toxicological analyses' without figures, favours breathing restriction and metabolic collapse during face-down restraint over a heart-rhythm death driven by stimulants while allowing the latter in some deaths, and reports, without figures, that restraint-related deaths are under-recorded in official statistics; in one Ontario series of 46 investigation reports, most deaths were classified as accidental or natural (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026). Both reviews are rated critically low for their methods, neither counts how often drugs caused or contributed to these deaths, and neither can show the cause of any single death. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.

set.statement: Excited delirium is a disputed label for extreme agitation, sometimes with stimulant drugs present. The two reviews considered here do not establish whether the described state kills independently of restraint, or how much deaths given the label were caused by restraint, drugs or both. They report no validated diagnostic criteria or specific autopsy/laboratory marker, and discuss the label as a diagnosis of exclusion (Strömmer et al., 2020; Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026). The 2020 review says forensic-pathology publications almost exclusively use excited delirium and describe fatal cases, while clinical publications use both excited and agitated delirium for survivors as well as deaths. This describes source types, not a count of which professionals apply the label. The 2026 review also describes a checklist used with living people in policing and prehospital care. It favours acute behavioral disturbance, retains the older term when citing its sources, and recommends replacement where possible; Strömmer’s team instead proposes agitated delirium with a modifier for restraint and a homicide or undetermined manner in restrained fatal cases. These are the authors’ recommendations, not conclusions tested by the data. Strömmer’s pooled analysis selected 168 individually described cases from 61 English-language reports/series found to 23 April 2020. Of 120 labelled excited delirium, 92 died; of 48 labelled agitated delirium, 12 died (unadjusted odds ratio 9.9). Some force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths and 43 of 64 survivors; none in 2 deaths and 1 survivor, and unknown in 8 deaths and 20 survivors. Force covers manual actions, handcuffs, hog/hobble ties, electrical weapons, sedation and other measures; it does not mean every case involved prone compression. These categories overlap. Cocaine was noted in 55 of 104 deaths and 19 of 64 survivors, as classified from case reports without standardized toxicology assessment or drug concentrations (Strömmer et al., 2020). The authors argue that restraint and the label are intertwined, and find no reliable evidence for an independent lethal syndrome. Their own limitations acknowledge nonrandom publication, overrepresentation and better documentation of deaths, and missing drug and restraint details. The editors’ appraisal is that source type, selection and clustering can connect the label, death and recorded force; the univariate analysis does not adjust for them. Only 3 cases explicitly had no force, and 28 had force status unknown, so neither absence of an independently lethal condition nor a causal death risk from restraint can be established. Some printed tables are internally inconsistent: Table 4 gives 100% mortality to a cited study whose title specifies non-fatal encounters. No corrected group fatality rate is supplied here; the later exchange is not part of the 2020 source (Strömmer et al., 2020). The 2026 narrative systematic review searched 2010–2025 and describes cocaine, methamphetamine and phencyclidine as frequently detected, without proportions or concentrations. It favours ventilatory compromise with metabolic collapse during prone restraint, but also allows stress/stimulant-associated arrhythmia in some deaths. It also cites case reports of deaths attributed to excited delirium without overt restraint. Attribution in those reports is not proof that the state itself caused death; the primary reports were not read. It describes volunteer experiments without clinically significant hypoxia or major circulatory compromise, and low mortality in some operational cohorts, while explaining why these do not reproduce all real-world conditions (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026, secondary summaries). For certification and counting, the 2026 review cites 46 Ontario investigation reports with most deaths classified accidental or natural and reports undercounting of restraint-related deaths without quantifying it. Its sources and methods are heterogeneous; the complete included-study set and supplement are unavailable here. The two reviews are rated critically low and overlap because the 2026 review cites Strömmer. They cannot quantify drug-caused deaths or give a causal verdict for an individual. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.

debate.question: Can the state labelled excited delirium cause death independently of restraint, or does the label conceal restraint-related deaths?
debate.evidence_yes: The 2026 review describes deaths attributed to the syndrome without overt restraint, and allows a stress-driven arrhythmic pathway with stimulant intoxication in some cases. The 2020 pooled set includes 2 deaths explicitly recorded without force, but its authors say their causes cannot be resolved. The 2026 review also relays healthy-volunteer and operational studies with no clinically important hypoxia or low mortality. These observations qualify a universal restraint explanation; none demonstrates an independent lethal syndrome. Cocaine was noted in 55 of 104 pooled deaths and 19 of 64 survivors, an unadjusted selected-case association rather than a drug effect (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026; Strömmer et al., 2020).
debate.evidence_no: The 2020 pooled reports link the excited label to death (92/120 versus 12/48 for agitated delirium), police as first authority (95/120 versus 16/48), handcuffs (80/120 versus 6/48) and hog/hobble ties (46/120 versus 1/48). Some force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths. The authors argue that this makes restraint a plausible explanation that the label can obscure. Their claim that previously published fatality figures under 10% and 8.3% trace to a source without mortality data is their citation-chain critique, not a newly verified primary finding here. The 2026 review describes rapid collapse after prone restraint in cited retrospective evidence: 58% of 229 deaths within 1–5 minutes, and breathing distress in at least 20%. At least one cited source concerns civil-litigation cases; the entire 229-case frame is not established from this review. It also reports non-specific biomarkers and favours a ventilatory/metabolic explanation (Strömmer et al., 2020; Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026).
debate.neither_can_show: The same presentation is labelled differently across source types. Forensic reports select deaths; clinical papers contain both survivors and deaths, not survivors alone. Publication, case selection, article clustering and documentation differ, and the pooled univariate analysis does not adjust for them. Force categories include sedation and electrical weapons as well as physical restraint, and missing force status is not absence of restraint. Drug categories do not provide a standardized concentration-based causal assessment. Volunteer findings do not reproduce every custodial setting, and selected death series cannot estimate the risk per encounter. Printed 2020 tables contain inconsistencies; later critiques/replies require their own full-source verification before their corrections or revised rates can be used. The 2026 supplement and several cited primary studies are unavailable. Neither review quantifies causal drug contributions or supplies an individual cause-of-death test.
debate.editors_reading: Editors’ reading (certainty: very low). The label describes a presentation; it does not by itself establish a cause. The evidence leaves both independently lethal agitation and restraint-related mechanisms unresolved at the population level. It does not justify treating stimulant detection as decisive or overlooking documented restraint. The 2 pooled deaths without force and secondary reports without overt restraint qualify claims that every death requires restraint, but do not prove the state alone caused death. Equally, the high frequency of recorded force does not establish the causal share of restraint. The 2026 review retains both physiological pathways and recommends independent investigation; Strömmer recommends a terminology/manner change. These are attributed recommendations, not a causal verdict.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Prospective linked police, ambulance, hospital and death-investigation records covering all severe-agitation encounters, fatal or not, with an outcome-independent case definition. Record restraint type, position, duration, compression, devices, sedation, initial rhythm, temperature, blood gases and timed toxicology, with independent autopsy and transparent attribution criteria. Reanalyse published cases by source type and article clustering, and verify the later exchange and primary reports before using corrected rates.

set.plain: What is excited delirium, and why is it disputed? It is a label for extreme agitation, used with living people as well as after deaths. These reviews report no agreed validated criteria or specific autopsy sign. In 168 published cases, force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths, but force included sedation and electrical weapons as well as being held down. Only 3 cases explicitly had no force; many had missing information. A later review also cites deaths attributed to the label without overt restraint. That does not prove what caused them. The selected reports cannot show how often restraint, drugs or the agitated state caused death. See the contested question.
set.magnitude: Selected individually described cases: 168 from 61 reports; 104 deaths, 64 survivors; excited 92/120 fatal versus agitated 12/48, unadjusted OR 9.9. Force: 94/104 deaths versus 43/64 survivors (editors subtraction from Table 2 none/unknown); none 2/1, unknown 8/20; total explicitly none 3, unknown 28. Police first 95/120 versus 16/48; handcuffs 80/120 versus 6/48; hog/hobble 46/120 versus 1/48. Cocaine noted 55/104 versus 19/64. These are selected-report associations, not causal effects or encounter rates. Secondary 2026 review: Finland 12/21,036 autopsies=0.06%; 229 deaths, 58% collapse within 1–5 min, at least 20% respiratory distress; Ontario 46 reports, most accidental/natural. No frequency of causal drug contribution. 2020 grouped rates are not repaired from unavailable later exchange.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Both reviews retain critically-low appraisals. Pooled cases are selected for publication; source type, case clustering, label and recording differ; analysis is univariate and several printed tables are inconsistent. The 2026 review does not identify the complete included set in its main article; primary studies and reviews may overlap, and a cited rapid-collapse source concerns litigation. Later exchange full texts and 2026 supplement are unavailable here.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Selected case/death reports are not a sample of all severe-agitation encounters. Clinical papers include both survivors and deaths. Force categories combine different actions and sedation; drug categories are taken from case descriptions without standardized concentrations. Volunteer data do not reproduce every real-world custodial circumstance.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: Only 3 pooled cases explicitly record no force, while 28 are unknown; no denominator of all encounters or count of causally drug-involved deaths. The 2 no-force deaths do not establish a mechanism.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; unchanged two-level risk-of-bias and one-level inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision downgrades reach the very-low floor. Status remains contested with all six debate fields. The 2026 review cites Strömmer, so they are not independent replication. Authors’ terminology recommendations differ; the newer review retains the old term for source fidelity and says replace where possible. Professional-body positions, primary no-restraint cases and later exchange content are not independently verified here. Draft retained.
